Family Health

An itchy penis: gentle care and when to get checked

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Genital itching is not always caused by an infection. Irritating products, skin conditions, parasites and sexually transmitted infections can produce overlapping symptoms. Gentle care can reduce discomfort, but ongoing itching, a new rash or other symptoms needs an assessment rather than a series of home remedies.

Begin with simple, gentle care

Pause fragranced washes, deodorants, antiseptics and any new product that seems to trigger symptoms. Wash gently with lukewarm water or a suitable soap substitute, then pat dry. Repeated washing and scrubbing can make irritated skin worse.

A cool, damp cloth held briefly against the outside skin may ease itching. Do not place ice directly on the penis. Cooling can soothe the sensation but does not treat scabies, a fungal infection or inflammation inside the urethra.

Wear comfortable, loose clothing and change out of sweaty clothes. Keep nails short, avoid scratching and pause shaving over irritated or broken skin. Do not pick or squeeze bumps that you think might be ingrown hairs.

If the foreskin retracts comfortably, clean gently beneath it and bring it forward again afterwards. Never force a tight foreskin back. Ask a pharmacist or clinician about a bland, fragrance-free emollient suitable for the affected area if the skin is dry.

Skip acidic and irritating remedies

Do not put apple cider vinegar, lemon juice, essential oils or disinfectant on genital skin. A diluted household product is not automatically safe for this sensitive area and may increase stinging, inflammation or skin injury.

Salt baths and homemade oatmeal mixtures should not be treated as proven cures for an unexplained genital rash. A product that is comfortable on an arm or leg may not be suitable for the head of the penis.

Avoid ordinary wart-removal liquids or freezing products on genital bumps. These are not designed for genital warts. Likewise, do not borrow a strong steroid cream prescribed for a different body site or another person.

Irritation, balanitis and skin conditions

Contact dermatitis can follow exposure to a cleanser, lubricant, condom ingredient or another irritant or allergen. Eczema can also affect genital skin; it is not simply an allergy in every case.

Balanitis means inflammation of the head of the penis, not inflammation of a gland. It may involve soreness, swelling, itching, discharge beneath the foreskin or discomfort when urinating. The treatment depends on whether irritation, yeast or another cause is present.

Psoriasis and lichen planus can occur on the penis. Genital psoriasis may look different from the thick, scaly plaques seen elsewhere. Lichen nitidus can cause tiny bumps and is another condition a clinician may consider.

These names cannot reliably be assigned from an online picture. Some normal skin features also look like bumps. A clinician or dermatologist can examine the pattern and, occasionally, arrange a small skin sample if the diagnosis remains uncertain.

Infections and parasites need specific treatment

Thrush can cause an itchy, sore head of the penis and irritation beneath the foreskin. It is not usually a sexually transmitted infection, and an antifungal will not help if the cause is dermatitis or another condition.

Genital herpes may begin with tingling or itching and can cause painful blisters or sores. Warts caused by HPV may itch or bleed, but not every genital bump is a wart. Seek assessment for new sores or bumps rather than trying to remove them yourself.

Scabies can cause marked itching, often worse at night, and may affect the penis as well as other areas. Pubic lice live on coarse hair and may cause itching around the pubic region. These require suitable treatment and advice about close contacts, clothing and bedding; soothing the skin alone will not eliminate them.

A rash on the groin crease or an inflamed hair follicle may have a different cause from a rash on the penis itself. Tell the clinician exactly where the itching occurs and whether other areas or close contacts are affected.

Other groin causes include folliculitis, meaning inflammation around a hair follicle; an ingrown hair after shaving; jock itch, a fungal rash usually affecting the groin folds; and molluscum contagiosum, a viral cause of small bumps. These may be confused with penile conditions and need different treatments. Once irritated skin has healed, avoiding a very close shave and shaving in the direction of hair growth can reduce recurrent ingrown hairs.

Get assessed if there are urinary or persistent symptoms

Burning during urination, discharge from the urethral opening or pain with sex can indicate urethritis or another infection. A sexual-health clinic can help, whether or not you know of a recent exposure.

Arrange a review when itching is severe, affects sleep, keeps returning or does not improve after removing likely irritants. New sores, bleeding, a persistent lump or skin changes that are not healing also need examination.

Fever, increasing pain, spreading swelling or feeling unwell calls for prompt advice. Seek emergency care if you cannot urinate, have sudden severe testicular pain or the foreskin is stuck behind the head of the penis.

A swab is not a single universal test for every cause. The clinician may use an examination, targeted swabs or urine tests, and sometimes other investigations. Recurrent or severe balanitis may prompt a check for contributing conditions such as diabetes.

Use the treatment intended for your diagnosis

A diagnosed inflammatory skin condition may need a prescribed steroid or another anti-inflammatory treatment. Genital skin absorbs medicines readily, so the strength, amount and duration should be clear. Stronger treatments sometimes have an appropriate specialist use; they should not be chosen casually for itch.

If an STI or a parasite is diagnosed, follow the advice about contacts and when sexual activity can resume. With an unexplained sore or possible STI, avoid contact that could transmit infection while awaiting assessment.

If a prescribed treatment burns, worsens the rash or fails to help, contact the prescriber. The goal is to identify and treat the cause while keeping the skin comfortable, not to suppress the symptom indefinitely.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NHS balanitis guidance recommends gentle washing, avoiding irritants and treatment tailored to the cause. Do not force a tight foreskin back.

The American Academy of Dermatology advises a specific plan for genital psoriasis because sensitive genital skin needs different treatment from many other body sites.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you prepare a list of products, symptoms and questions for a clinician. An examination may be needed to distinguish skin inflammation, infection and normal skin features.

When to seek help

Seek urgent care for inability to urinate, sudden severe testicular pain or a foreskin trapped behind the head of the penis. Persistent sores, bleeding, discharge and worsening swelling need assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Use gentle cleansing and avoid scratching or excessive washing.
  • Do not apply vinegar, household acids or ordinary wart products to genital skin.
  • Skin conditions, infection and parasites require different treatment.
  • New sores, discharge, urinary pain or persistent changes need assessment.
  • Use genital steroid treatments only with a clear diagnosis and instructions.

Frequently asked questions

Can a cold cloth cure the cause of itching?

No. It may ease discomfort temporarily, but an infection or skin condition may still need treatment.

Does genital itching always mean an STI?

No. Irritation, eczema and other non-sexually transmitted conditions are also possible.

Can I use my usual psoriasis cream on the penis?

Check first. Thin genital skin may need a different medicine or schedule from other parts of the body.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
